newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn fails again to reach deal on budget, gold.
newsitem.headline: Bonn fails again to reach deal on budget, gold.

text.p: The German government on Tuesday failed for the third time in three days to agree on ways to plug gaping budget holes and came under growing pressure to scrap a controversial plan to grab Bundesbank gold reserves this year.

As Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and the Free Democrats (FDP) coalition partners remained deadlocked over deficit-ridden budgets, more voices from within the coalition began speaking out against Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue central bank assets against its will.
"There is an impression that no one knows how we can get out of this financial dilemma without endangering the coalition," said one CDU official after the fruitless coalition meeting.

The CDU official, speaking on the condition that he not be named, said many conservative deputies were objecting to Waigel's plans to revalue reserves against the central bank's will in order to book profits of 20 billion marks ($11.6 billion) this year.
The revaluation in 1997 could help Germany meet the criteria to qualify for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

He added there were growing doubts in the CDU that the party could muster enough votes to pass Waigel's proposed law. The centre-right coalition has a slim 12-seat majority and several CDU and FDP deputies said they won't oppose the Bundesbank.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer arrived at the Finance Ministry in Bonn at midday to discuss the plan with Waigel.

The beleaguered finance minister, who was berated by his leaders from his CSU party in Munich on Monday for resorting to budget tricks, has said he wants to reach a consensus agreement with the powerful central bank.

The central bank is not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insists that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of the CDU, told ZDF television that the government was working towards a consensus with the Bundesbank.

"We are in the middle of negotiations and very interested in coming to a consensus agreement with the Bundesbank on the revaluation of the gold reserves," Hintze said. "We are striving to reach an agreement and I am confident we will reach one."
The Bundesbank has repeatedly warned Bonn against resorting to tricks designed to squeeze Germany into currency union.

Still angered by Waigel's plan to revalue national gold and currency reserves and use a part of those proceeds to fill budget holes this year, the Bundesbank compared Bonn's plans to practices Bonn itself had disapproved of when proposed by other governments.

"A transfer of funds from a revalution in 1997 could be seen as creative accounting," Bundesbank official Helmut Hesse said in Hanover, recalling Germany's disdain when Italy and France gained approval for one-off measures to meet EMU goals.

Hintze told ZDF television even though some CDU deputies in parliament have said they would not vote for a law on the gold revaluation against the will of the Bundesbank he was confident that there would be no defections once an agreement was reached.

"If we reach a consensus with the Bundesbank, and the finance minister is trying with all his energy to reach such a consensus, there won't be any defectors because who is going to have something against a consensus between the Bundesbank and government," Hintze said.

To plug the deficit holes, Waigel reportedly wants to raise petrol taxes or delay the reduction in the 7.5 percent solidarity income tax surcharge to fill the holes -- proposals the FDP strictly opposes.

An FDP official it was "inconceivable" that the FDP would agree to CDU demands to raise taxes to plug the budget deficits. The budget hole for 1997 is now projected to be at least 20 to 25 billion marks.

A prominent young leader of Kohl's CDU urged the government not to raise taxes to fill huge gaps in its 1997 budget. Christian Wulff, CDU leader in Lower Saxony state, said Waigel should slash state spending rather than increase taxes.

"The tax burden has reached the maximum point for achievers and skilled workers in this society," Wulff told the Chemnitz daily Freie Presse. "Something is wrong in this country." ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
